Dual Palladium/Photoredox-Catalyzed Enantioselective and
Regioselective Decarboxylative Hydroaminoalkylation of Allenes
Jun Zheng, Ali Nikbakht, and Bernhard Breit *
Cite This: ACS Catal. 2021, 11, 3343 −3350 Read Online
ACCESS Metrics & More Article Recommendations *sı Supporting Information
ABSTRACT: A dual palladium/photoredox-catalyzed regio- and enantioselective decarboxylative hydroaminoalkylation of allenes
with amino acids is reported. This mild, redox-neutral, and atom-economic process allows access to a range of protected vinyl 1,2-
amino ethers in good yields with high levels of branched and enantioselectivity, when alkoxyallenes were employed. Conversely, with
alkyl- and aryl-substituted terminal allenes as the substrates, a linear-selective decarboxylative hydroaminoalkylation of allenes is
realized in high regio- and E/Z selectivities with a Pd/ rac-BINAP catalytic system.
KEYWORDS: α-amino acid, allene, palladium, photoredox, chiral vicinal amino alcohol
C
hiral 1,2-amino alcohols have emerged as a common motif
in a variety of diﬀerent natural products and pharmaceuti-
cally active compounds as well as privileged chiral auxiliaries and
ligands (Figure 1). As a result, the importance of vicinal amino
alcohols has stimulated extensive e ﬀort from the synthetic
community toward their synthesis.
1 Among them, processes that
form the C −C bond between the amine and alcohol
functionalities are particularly attractive but challenging using
typical two-electron ionic processes ( Scheme 1A).
Therefore, a traditional reverse polarity (Umpolung) strategy,
such as using nitroalkane nucleophiles as carbanion equivalents,
has been proposed for addressing this issue.
2 Despite their
eﬀectiveness, these methods often require subsequent refunc-
tionalization to deliver the amine. The direct enantioselective α-
lithiation of alkylamines for the addition to carbonyls is an
alternative, which neverthel ess often requires cryogenic
conditions, the use of stoichiometric amounts of sparteine and
strong bases (alkyl lithiums).
3 Hence, developing a streamlined,
eﬃcient, and atom-economic methodology to enable the
enantioselective construction of vicinal amino alcohols via a
C−C bond formation process under ambient conditions is
highly demanded.
In recent years, radical cross-coupling between amine and
alcohol moieties for the construction of vicinal amino alcohols
by photoredox catalysis has received widespread attention.
4
However, only a few examples of asymmetric photoredox
catalysis to access enantioenriched this class of compounds have
been reported,
5 including chiral phosphoric acid organo-
catalysts,6 chiral-at-metal rhodium/iridium complex,7 and chiral
scandium-N,N′-dioxide complex. 8 Furthermore, long-living
ketyl radicals obtained from a reduction of aromatic carbonyls
are required for a successful radical cross-coupling in all of these
methods, which diminish the generality of the scope. Therefore,
exploring alternative alcohol moieties that can enable versatile
further transformations and e ﬀectively couple with α-amino
alkyl radicals is highly desirable.
Alkoxyallenes are versatile building blocks for organic
synthesis, especially serving as atom-economic
9 π-allyl fragment
precursors for palladium-catalyzed allylic addition to pronu-
cleophiles leading to allylic alcohol building blocks.
10 However,
the current state of the art to access C−C bonds is still restricted
to the allylation with soft carbon nucleophiles, such as
Meldrum’s acids,
11 azlactones,12 oxindoles,13 and pyrazolones14
(Scheme 1B). To broaden the carbon pronucleophiles window
of hydroalkylation of allenes, we recently described a rhodium/
photoredox co-catalyzed atom-economic regiodivergent hydro-
aminoalkylation of alkynes and allenes, but unfortunately only
racemic homoallylic amines could be obtained.
15

Inspired by these advances as well as recent progress in
enantioselective metallaphotoredox catalysis, 5 we envisioned
that the utility of alkoxyallenes as the allylic precursor in the
cross-coupling with α-amino alkyl radicals could lead to the
formation of 1,2-amino ethers ( Scheme 1C). In addition, easy-
to-access α-amino acids, which are widely used to generate α-
amino alkyl radicals via a single-electron-oxidative decarbox-
ylation process, 16 could be suitable substrates for the hydro-
aminoalkylation of allenes because α-amino acids can
simultaneously serve as reductants and a proton source. The
released proton from the decarboxylation of α-amino acids
could promote the generation of a palladium(II) hydride

species, which is crucial for the formation of a π-allyl palladium
intermediate from allenes. Moreover, the π-allyl palladium
species is believed to be the key intermediate to control
reactivity, regioselectivity, and stereoselectivity.
17 After being
attacked by the activated α-amino alkyl radical and one electron
reduction, the desired 1,2-amino alcohol function might be
obtained. Herein, we report on an enantioselective decarbox-
ylative hydroaminoalkylation of allenes with α-amino acids via a
combined palladium and photoredox catalysis to give facile
access to syn-vicinal amino alcohols with high levels of regio- and
enantiocontrol.
We began our studies by reacting N-phenyl-protected phenyl
alanine (1a) and cyclohexyloxyallene (2a) in the presence of 2.5
mol % of [Pd
2(dba)3], 6 mol % ( S)-BINAP, 50 mol % p-
CF3C6H4COOH, 1 mol % [Ir(ppy) 2(dtbbpy)PF6][ PC1], and
D M Fa ss o l v e n t su n d e rb l u e l ight-emitting-diode (LED)
irradiation. After 16 h, the desired product 3aa was obtained
in good yields, with >19:1 B/L but poor diastereo- and
enantiocontrol (1.3:1 dr, 69:31 er).
18 To our delight, further
ligand screening revealed that the Feringa ligand (L9) proved to
be optimal, aﬀording product 3aa with 72% yield, 86:14 B/L, 4:1
dr, and 97:3 er (Table 1, entry 1).18 A survey of solvents and acid
additives was conducted, however, without bene ﬁcial results.18
Interestingly, evaluation of diﬀerent photosensitizers resulted in
a slight improvement in regioselectivity (90:10 B/L) using
[Ir(dF(CF
3)ppy)2(dtbbpy)PF6][ PC2] as the photocatalyst,
while maintaining reactivity (70% yield) and stereoselectivity
(4.5:1 dr, 96:4 er) ( Table 1, entries 2 and 3). Variation of the
photocatalyst loading revealed that 1 mol % provided optimal
results ( Table 1 , entries 4 −5). Finally, control experiments
demonstrated that photocatalyst, palladium catalyst, and blue
LED are all crucial for this decarboxylative α-allylation reaction
(Table 1, entries 6 −8).
With the optimized reaction conditions in hand, the substrate
scope with respect to the two reaction partners was investigated.
First, we explored N-phenyl-protected amino acids derived from
natural and unnatural amino acids. As summarized in Table 2,a
wide range of branched allylated 1,2-amino ethers can readily be
obtained in good yields with high regio- and enantioselectivities.
In addition to O-tert-butyl-tyrosine, unprotected tyrosine was
also found to be a suitable substrate yielding the allylation
adduct ( 3ca) with 91:9 regioselectivity and 96:4 enantiomeric
ratio, as well as complete chemoselectivity in favor of carbon −
carbon bond formation instead of the phenol acting as an oxygen
nucleophile. A 2-naphthyl alanine derivative was allylated well in
this Pd/Ir dual catalytic system, a ﬀording the corresponding
product 3da in 74% yield with 96:4 er. Furthermore, a
tryptophan derivative with an unprotected indole moiety
coupled well to furnish allylation adduct 3ea in good yield and
high control of regio- and enantioselectivities. Other N-phenyl-
derived amino acids with aliphatic side chains, including alanine,
2-aminobutanoic acid, norval ine, and leucine, were also
successfully allylated, yielding the related 1,2-amino ethers
(3fa−3ja)i n4 1 −55% yields with high regio- and enantiose-
lectivity. In addition, N-phenyl amino acids bearing other
functional groups such as OBn, O
tBu, SMe, and carboxylate
esters, involving serine, methionine, aspartic acid, and glutamic
a c i d ,w e r ea l s oc o m p a t i b l ei nt h i sh y d r o a m i n o a l k y l a t i o n
reaction. In all cases, the products ( 3ka−3oa) were obtained
in moderate diastereoselectivity with high regio- and enantio-
control. To be noted, a cyclic amino acid derived from proline
coupled well with the allene, resulting in a tertiary homoallylic
amine (3pa) in 93:7 er.
As demonstrated in Table 3, with N-phenyl-protected phenyl
alanine (1a) as the coupling partner under the standard reaction
conditions, the transformation worked well for a range of
alkoxyallenes. The enantioselective hydroaminoalkylation of
cyclopentyl, cycloheptyl, (trimethylsilyl)ethyl, and nonyl-oxy-
allenes also proceeded smoothly to furnish the corresponding
allylated adducts ( 3ab−3ae) in good yields (71 −78% yields)
and diastereoselectivity (2.7:1 −5.6:1 dr) with high regio-
(91:9−>95:5 B/L) and enantiocontrol (89:11 −97:3 er). A
number of benzyloxyallene derivatives reacted well with amino
acid 1a leading to the desired products (3af−3ai) in good yields
and regio- and enantioselectivities. Using the bulkier 1,1-
dimethylpropyloxyallene and tert-butyl-oxyallene, the yields of
related products ( 3aj−3ak) slightly decreased, while the
enantioselectivity remained high. Gratifyingly, alkoxyallene
bearing a chiral alkoxyl group on the side chain underwent
this allylation reaction well to give the corresponding product
3al in 83% yield with >19:1 dr for the syn-isomer using ent-L9 as
the ligand. To investigate the matched/mismatched eﬀect of this
transformation, L9 was used as a ligand for this hydro-
aminoalkylation reaction, and reversed diastereoselectivities
were observed, indicating that the stereochemical induction in
this cross-coupling reaction was mostly controlled by the chiral
ligand rather than the chiral substrate. To be noted, 1,1 ′-
disubstituted alkoxylallene ( 2m) was also applicable in this
transformation.

According to previous observations on palladium-catalyzed
addition of pronucleophiles into allenes, 20 by switching the
ligand to rac-BINAP, to our delight, the alkyl-substituted
terminal allenes coupled well with amino acids, leading to an
array of homoallylic amines ( 4a−4j, 4l−4t) with exclusive
linear- and E/Z selectivities ( Table 4 ). The terminal allenes
containing various functional groups, such as OH, OTBS,
phthalimide, and alkene, were well tolerated in this trans-
formation. The phenyl allene coupled well in this trans-
formation, although the related product ( 4k) could only be
obtained in a modest L/B ratio. Satisfyingly, the reactions with
PMP-protected amino acids performed well, i.e., delivered the
desired adducts (4s−4t) with up to 90% yields. The generality of
this transformation o ﬀers a direct and e ﬃcient strategy to
prepare homoallylic amines.
Furthermore, the practical utility of this methodology was
highlighted by several postcatalysis transformations of the
furnished products ( Scheme 2). Compound 3al was subjected
to acidic conditions to generate the chiral vicinal amino alcohol
5a in 85% yield with 99:1 er. Hydrogenation of 3ag with Pd/C
under H 2 (1 atm) at ambient temperature followed by
subsequent treatment with triﬂuoroacetic acid (TFA) furnished
the secondary alcohol 5b in a good yield. Hydroboration and
consecutive oxidation of 3aa gave the 1,4-amino alcohol 5c in
63% yield. Rhodium-catalyzed hydroformylation of 3aa could
form a six-membered cyclized enamine, which could be
hydrogenated in situ a ﬀording 2,3-disubstituted piperidine
(5d) in 60% yield over two steps.
To gain some insights into the mechanism, a series of
experiments were carried out (see the Supporting Information).
The addition of a radical scavenger (TEMPO) could inhibit the
reaction completely, which indicated the prevalence of a free-
radical pathway. Furthermore, a radical trap experiment was
conducted with the addition of ethyl acrylate, and the α-
alkylated product was formed through an α-amino alkyl radical
via a Giese-type reaction. The application of N-phenyl amino
acid (L-1a)o r( D-1a) derived from enantiomerically pure phenyl
alanine in this transformation leads to the same regio- and
stereoselectivities. The coupling reaction between 1a and
cyclohexyl allene under the linear-selective reaction conditions
produced a dimer compound from 1a. Those observations also
support the formation of an intermediate α-amino alkyl radical.
Stern−Volmer studies of N-phenyl amino acid ( 1a) with
photocatalyst [PC1] revealed that a simpleN-phenyl amino acid

(1a) was not able to quench the photoexcited Ir III complex,
while basifying 1a with Cs 2CO3 could e ﬀectively undergo a
reductive quenching process. Although there was no base
additive in the reaction system, the formation of π-allyl
palladium intermediate from allenes will promote the deproto-
nation of amino acids, which also hints that a π-allyl palladium
intermediate is formed prior to the single-electron decarbox-
ylation of amino acids. Furthermore, the low quantum yield
suggested that a radical-chain propagation mechanism was not
involved in this reaction.
18 In addition, the importance of
irradiation throughout the reaction was further veriﬁed by a light
on/oﬀ experiment. When monitoring the reaction by 1H NMR
within the ﬁrst 1 h, a fast addition of the carboxylic acid to allene
forming the ester 5aa was observed. This suggested that the
oxidative decarboxylation occurs after this ester formation.
Based on these mechanistic studies and previous reports, a
potential mechanism for this decarboxylative hydroaminoalky-
lation is proposed ( Scheme 3). This transformation starts from
the oxidative addition of palladium catalyst with amino acid
generating the palladium hydride species A. Then, migratory
insertion of the intermediate A to the allene generates the π-allyl
palladium species B, which then undergoes competing pathways
between a fast reductive elimination leading to an ester
intermediate ( 5aa) and a relatively slow decarboxylation via a
reductive quenching process of the blue-light-excited Ir(III) *
complex. A recent report from the Tunge group21 suggested that
in this process, a single electron transfer from the carboxylate to
Pd in intermediate C can facilitate the decarboxylation process
and the newly formed carbon radical then rebounds with the π-
allyl-Pd species, resulting in the formation of intermediate D.
The π-allyl palladium(III) species D undergoes reductive
elimination forging the formation of a new C −C bond and a
Pd(I) species. The catalytic cycle ﬁnishes with the regeneration
of Pd(0) via the reduction of Pd(I) by the Ir(II) complex.
To conclude, we developed an asymmetric dual photoredox/
palladium-catalyzed decarboxylative hydroaminoalkylation of
alkoxylallenes to give synthetically useful protected vinyl 1,2-
amino alcohol products with high degrees of regio- and
enantioselectivities. A variety of common protecting groups as
well as a broad range of protected amino acids bearing di ﬀerent
functional groups were applicable. Mechanistic experiments
demonstrated that oxidative decarboxylation might occur after
the ester formation of allenes with amino acids, which is also in
accordance with the observation of speci ﬁc chemoselectivity in
the reaction with tyrosine. This transformation enables a
diﬀerent retrosynthetic strategy for accessing enantioenriched
1,2-amino alcohols, complementing the traditional two-electron
polarity reversal approaches. With alkyl- and aryl-substituted
terminal allenes as the substrates, linear-selective decarbox-
ylative hydroaminoalkylation is realized in high levels of regio-
and E/Z selectivities with a Pd/ rac-BINAP catalytic system. To
the best of our knowledge, this transformation represents a rare
example of asymmetric hydroaminoalkylation of allenes. Further
studies to apply this strategy to synthesize other important
bioactive compounds and potential drug candidates are
currently ongoing in our laboratory.
